task_brief: Day 6 of "Algorithms and Programming Structures" (unit 2, grade 7) is a correction and reflection on functions and debugging. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 40–60 minutes. The unit is working toward: Build a small interactive program and document tests, bugs, and revisions. Today's work contributes to that by handling functions and debugging at the correction and reflection stage, against the unit's wider topics of decomposition, pseudocode, variables and data types, and conditionals. This session produces reviewable evidence toward the unit performance task.
primary_task: Correct and reflect on your own earlier work involving functions and debugging. Build a defect log: one row per error, giving the symptom you or the check observed, the root cause you diagnosed, the specific change that fixed it, and the check that now passes. Include at least one case that failed before the fix and passes after it. Then write what pattern connects your errors — a misread condition, a skipped verification, an assumption about functions and debugging — and name one habit that would catch that pattern earlier next time. The activity_setup block below supplies the complete central input, exact specification, execution method, test cases, debugging target, and equal-credit manual simulation; use those exact materials rather than waiting for another handout, account, service, or tool. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about functions and debugging, and it belongs to "Algorithms and Programming Structures", which also covers separate topics such as decomposition. Close out with this check before you stop: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about functions and debugging; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. At grade 7 the bar is independent work with reasoning that a reader can follow without you present, plus one stated check you ran on your own result before submitting.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

remediation: Reteaching for functions and debugging follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for functions and debugging, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for functions and debugging works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of functions and debugging, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking functions and debugging mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply functions and debugging under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on functions and debugging rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
